objectives: Trace the hominin lineage from Sahelanthropus through modern Homo sapiens.
Explain the recent African origin model and the role of Neanderthal + Denisovan admixture.
Identify documented signatures of recent positive selection on the human genome.

slides.title: The hominin lineage: from Sahelanthropus to Homo
slides.body:
**Hominins** = the clade containing modern humans + all extinct relatives more closely related to humans than to chimpanzees (the chimp-human split is ~6-7 Mya per molecular clocks). The hominin fossil record now spans ~7 million years and includes >20 named species — most extinct, only one (Homo sapiens) extant.

**Sahelanthropus tchadensis** (Brunet et al. 2002 *Nature*) — Toumaï, found in Chad. ~7 Mya, near the chimp-human divergence. Cranial morphology suggests bipedalism (anterior position of foramen magnum). Debated whether it is on the human or panin (chimp) line, or near the common ancestor.

**Orrorin tugenensis** (Senut, Pickford 2001) — Kenya, ~6 Mya. Femoral morphology suggests bipedalism. Pre-Lucy hominin.

**Ardipithecus ramidus** ('Ardi'; White, Suwa, Lovejoy 2009 *Science* series) — Aramis, Ethiopia, ~4.4 Mya. Partial skeleton; mosaic of climbing + bipedal traits. Reframed views of last common ancestor as not chimp-like (forested arboreal-and-terrestrial).

**Australopithecus afarensis** — Donald Johanson + Tom Gray, **'Lucy'** discovered 24 November 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia. ~3.2 Mya, ~40% complete skeleton. Definitively bipedal (pelvis, knee, foot anatomy; Laetoli footprints, Mary Leakey 1976, ~3.7 Mya confirm species-level bipedalism). Brain ~400-500 cc (chimp range). Donald Johanson's *Lucy: The Beginnings of Humankind* (1981) the popular account. Lived ~3.9-3.0 Mya in East Africa. Likely tool-maker (Lomekwi tools 3.3 Mya, Harmand 2015).

**Other australopithecines** — *A. africanus* (Taung child, Raymond Dart 1924 — first African hominin recognized), *A. sediba* (Berger 2008-2010), *A. anamensis*. Many sympatric species; East and Southern African distribution.

**Paranthropus** (= robust australopithecines): *P. boisei*, *P. robustus*, *P. aethiopicus*. ~2.6-1.2 Mya. Massive jaws + sagittal crest; herbivorous high-fiber diet. Sister lineage to *Homo*; ultimately extinct.

**Homo habilis** (Leakey 1964) — ~2.4-1.4 Mya. Olduvai. First Homo; ~600-700 cc brain. Made Oldowan stone tools (sharp flakes; 2.6 Mya at Gona, Semaw 1997).

**Homo erectus** (s.l.) — 2.0 Mya - 100 kya. First hominin out of Africa (Dmanisi, Georgia 1.8 Mya; Java; Zhoukoudian China). ~900-1100 cc brain. Acheulean tools (handaxes ~1.6 Mya, Le Boueri Tabba). Long-lived species. Includes Dmanisi (early African), *Homo ergaster* (debated synonym), Java, Peking. Survived ~2 Myr — longer than any other Homo species.

**Homo heidelbergensis** (or *H. rhodesiensis*) — ~700-200 kya. Common ancestor of Neanderthals + modern humans + Denisovans (per Stringer + Hublin). African heidelbergensis → Homo sapiens; Eurasian heidelbergensis → Neanderthals + Denisovans. Brain ~1200 cc.

**Homo neanderthalensis** — ~430-40 kya, Eurasia (from Iberia to Altai). Adapted to cold; ~1500 cc brain (larger than modern human average!); muscular; complex tools (Mousterian); buried dead (debated extent); art (Spanish caves, Hoffmann 2018 dating); interbred with modern humans.

**Denisovans** — known mainly from genomic data + a few teeth + a finger bone from Denisova Cave (Altai). Identified by Pääbo's group via DNA sequencing (Reich, Pääbo, Krause 2010 *Nature*). Sister to Neanderthals; diverged ~400-500 kya. Lived across Asia + Oceania. **Svante Pääbo** awarded the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for genomes of extinct hominins.

**Homo sapiens** — anatomically modern humans. Oldest fossils: Jebel Irhoud, Morocco ~315 kya (Hublin 2017 *Nature*) — earlier than the previous Omo Kibish ~195 kya. Behavioral modernity (symbolic culture, complex tools, art) appears unevenly between 200-50 kya across Africa; clear out-of-Africa expansion ~60-70 kya.

**Other species** — *Homo floresiensis* ('hobbit', Flores, Indonesia, 100-50 kya; ~400 cc); *Homo luzonensis* (Luzon, Philippines, ~50 kya); *Homo naledi* (Rising Star, South Africa, ~250 kya); *Homo longi* ('Dragon Man', China, debated). At least 9-10 hominin species coexisted at various times in the last 1 Myr.

slides.title: Out of Africa, mitochondrial Eve, and admixture
slides.body:
**Recent African Origin (RAO) / Out-of-Africa (OOA) model** — modern humans (Homo sapiens) originated in Africa, expanded out ~60-70 kya, and largely replaced (with some admixture) other Eurasian hominins. Articulated by Christopher Stringer, Günter Bräuer, Allan Wilson + Rebecca Cann + Mark Stoneking, Lucotte, others.

**Mitochondrial Eve** — Cann, Stoneking, Wilson 1987 *Nature* 'Mitochondrial DNA and human evolution'. Sampled mtDNA from ~150 humans across continents; built a tree; the deepest branches were African. The most recent common ancestor of all human mtDNA lineages — 'mitochondrial Eve' — lived in Africa ~150-200 kya. (Wilson's lab; A. C. Wilson — Sarich's collaborator on the chimp-human molecular clock work.) Confirms Africa as the cradle of modern humans.

**Y-chromosomal Adam** — analogous calculation on Y chromosome; coalesces ~200-300 kya, also in Africa.

**Whole-genome data** confirm the OOA model: non-African populations are a subset of the African genetic diversity. Pairwise diversity (heterozygosity) is highest in African populations (~0.001) and decreases stepwise as one moves geographically further from Africa — the 'serial founder effect' signature. The bottleneck of the OOA migration (~60-70 kya) left a residue of low diversity outside Africa.

**Neanderthal admixture** — Pääbo lab. **Neanderthal draft genome** (Green et al. 2010 *Science*) from Vindija + Mezmaiskaya bones. Shocking result: 1-4% of the DNA of non-African modern humans is Neanderthal in origin. Mostly absent from Sub-Saharan Africans (though some back-flow has now been detected — Chen 2020). Implies modern humans interbred with Neanderthals in Eurasia ~50-60 kya (Sankararaman 2012 dated the introgression). Neanderthal alleles affect modern human skin pigmentation, immune function (TLR loci, OAS antiviral cluster — Quach 2016), high-altitude EPAS1 (in Tibetans; but that's Denisovan), metabolic traits, and some disease risk.

**Denisovan admixture** — Reich + Pääbo + Patterson + Krause 2010-2014. Denisovans contribute ~3-6% to Melanesian + Papuan genomes; ~0.2% to East Asian; trace amounts in South Asia + South America. The famous Tibetan **EPAS1** high-altitude allele was introgressed from Denisovans (Huerta-Sánchez et al. 2014 *Nature*). Australian Aboriginal + Papuan ancestors interbred with Denisovans ~45 kya in island Southeast Asia.

**Ghost lineages** — admixture from unsampled archaic populations is increasingly detected (Mondal 2019; Hammer 2011 'archaic admixture in African populations'). The human lineage is reticulate, not a clean tree.

**Multi-regional model** (Wolpoff, Thorne, Wu) — once a leading alternative: modern humans evolved in parallel across the Old World from regional Homo erectus populations with gene flow. Refuted by genomic data; only modest admixture supports it, not parallel evolution.

**Recent African demography** — Africa has 3-5× more genetic diversity than non-Africa; was structured into deeply divergent populations long before OOA. Lipson + Reich, Skoglund + Mathieson, Schlebusch, Tishkoff labs reconstructing this with ancient DNA + modern genomes.

**David Reich** (Harvard, HHMI) — co-author with Pääbo on Neanderthal + Denisovan papers; ancient DNA pioneer. *Who We Are and How We Got Here* (2018) — popular synthesis. Reich's lab has sequenced thousands of ancient genomes worldwide, transforming the field.

**Svante Pääbo** — Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Leipzig. *Neanderthal Man* (2014). Founded ancient DNA as a field (pioneering authentication, contamination control). Nobel 2022 Physiology or Medicine. **Mark Stoneking** + **Rebecca Cann** — co-authors on the mtEve paper (1987) with Wilson. Foundational for human population genetics.

slides.title: Selection on the human genome: lactase, pigmentation, altitude, malaria
slides.body:
Recent positive selection — selection acting in the last ~10-50 kya — leaves detectable genomic signatures (extended haplotype homozygosity, low diversity around the sweep, derived-allele excess). Scans (Voight + Pritchard 2006 iHS; Sabeti EHH 2002, XP-EHH 2007; Tang FST; composite Grossman CMS 2010) have identified hundreds of candidate loci.

**Lactase persistence** — most adult mammals (including humans) downregulate lactase (LCT) after weaning, becoming lactose-intolerant. In populations with long dairying histories (Northern Europeans, East African pastoralists, some Arabian populations), regulatory mutations upstream of LCT (in the *MCM6* intron) maintain lactase into adulthood. The European allele (rs4988235, T allele) is at >90% frequency in Scandinavians, 0% in East Asians. East Africans (Maasai, Tutsi) carry independent mutations at *different* sites (Tishkoff 2007 *Nature Genet*) — convergent evolution. Selection coefficients estimated s ≈ 0.05-0.10 — among the strongest selection ever measured in humans. Dating: emerged ~5-10 kya, coincident with cattle domestication (Burger 2007 'lactase persistence among Neolithic Europeans'). Ancient DNA shows the allele was rare in early European farmers; rose to dominance after the Bronze Age (Mathieson 2015).

**Skin pigmentation** — light skin in non-tropical populations is convergently selected via different genes. **SLC24A5** (rs1426654, A111T) — Lamason et al. 2005 *Science* identified zebrafish *golden* mutant ortholog; the derived allele is at ~99% frequency in Europeans, >75% in Middle Easterners + South Asians, 0% in West Africans. Selection coefficient ~0.04. **SLC45A2**, **TYR**, **TYRP1**, **KITLG**, **OCA2/HERC2** (eye color), **MFSD12** (Crawford 2017 *Science* on African skin pigmentation) — each contributes. Light skin allows efficient UVB-driven vitamin D synthesis at high latitudes (Loomis 1967; Jablonski + Chaplin 2000). Selection acted in last 5-10 kya as agriculture moved populations into high-latitude vitamin-D-limited environments.

**EPAS1 in Tibetans** — Yi + Wang + Cui 2010 *Science*; Huerta-Sánchez 2014 *Nature*. Tibetans live at ~4000 m with lower polycythemic response (less elevated hemoglobin) than acclimatized lowlanders — the lowland response is maladaptive long-term. The derived EPAS1 haplotype (HIF-2α gene; oxygen-sensing) is at ~87% frequency in Tibetans, 9% in Han Chinese, 0% elsewhere. **The haplotype is Denisovan-introgressed** — one of the most striking adaptive-introgression examples in any species. Selection s ≈ 0.03-0.06 over ~6 kya since the agriculture-driven Tibetan plateau colonization.

**Sickle cell + malaria** — HbS (β-globin S allele) — Allison 1954. Heterozygote advantage against *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria. Other malaria-protective alleles: HbC (West African), HbE (Southeast Asian), Duffy-null (*FY*BES blocks *P. vivax*; ~100% in West Africans), G6PD deficiency (X-linked; ~20% of males in malarial regions), α + β-thalassemias (Mediterranean, SE Asia). Convergent evolution against the same pathogen via at least ~10 different alleles — one of the strongest selection signatures in the human genome (Kwiatkowski 2005; Hedrick 2011).

**Other selection signals** — *FOXP2* (language; though selection-strength estimates are now debated, Atkinson 2018); *ADH1B* alcohol metabolism (East Asia); *PLN/CCR5*-Δ32 (immune; the famous HIV-resistance allele); *AMY1* salivary amylase copy-number (high in starch-rich diets, Perry 2007); cold adaptation in Inuit (Fumagalli 2015 *Science*); diving response in Bajau sea nomads (Ilardo 2018).

**Pardis Sabeti** (Harvard / Broad) — developed EHH-based tests for recent positive selection (Sabeti 2002, 2007). Applied to scan for sweeps across populations + diseases. Composite of Multiple Signals (CMS; Grossman + Sabeti 2010, 2013) integrates multiple statistics. Sabeti's lab tracks pathogen + host coevolution (Lassa, Ebola, HIV, malaria).

**Jonathan Pritchard** (Stanford, HHMI) — developed iHS (integrated Haplotype Score; Voight + Pritchard 2006), STRUCTURE software (Pritchard 2000) for population-structure inference. Pritchard's recent work has emphasized that classic hard sweeps may be rarer than once thought in humans — **polygenic adaptation** on standing variation across many small-effect loci is the dominant mode (next lesson, Berg + Coop, Pritchard 2017 reviews).

Human evolution did not stop at the OOA migration. The last 10 kya — agriculture, urbanization, latitude shifts, pathogens — drove some of the strongest selection signals ever measured in any species.

question.question: Estimate when mitochondrial Eve lived
question.goal: Use mitochondrial divergence + mutation rate to bracket the human mtDNA TMRCA.

steps.prompt: Cann + Stoneking + Wilson (1987) estimated mean human mtDNA pairwise divergence d ≈ 0.0036 (substitutions per site) using restriction-enzyme data. The mtDNA mutation rate is μ ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁸ per site per year (modern estimates; original 1987 estimate was higher). Compute the apparent coalescent time T = d / (2μ) in years.
steps.motivation: Pairwise divergence accumulates on both lineages.
steps.reveal: T = 0.0036 / (2 × 2 × 10⁻⁸) = 0.0036 / (4 × 10⁻⁸) = 9 × 10⁴ = 90000 years. This is an underestimate because mtDNA rate is heterogeneous + saturation effects. Better estimates (Soares 2009; Fu 2013 using ancient mtDNAs as calibrators) put mt-Eve at ~150-200 kya.

steps.prompt: Why does mt-Eve coalesce ~150-200 kya rather than ~6-7 Mya (chimp-human split)?
steps.motivation: Coalescent reduces TMRCA below speciation date.

acceptedAnswers: TMRCA within a species ≈ 2N_e (for mtDNA, N_e of females ≈ 5000-7000); much less than time to chimp-human split

steps.reveal: TMRCA = 2N_e (for haploid mtDNA, N_e is the effective female population size, ≈ 5000-7000 for humans). 2 × 7000 × ~25 yr/generation ≈ 350000 yr — same order as 150-200 kya. Importantly, this is **within-species** coalescence — the species itself is older (Homo sapiens originated ~300 kya from heidelbergensis stock), and the lineage is older still. Mt-Eve was a regular member of an existing population; her status is statistical, not unique.

steps.prompt: Why is mt-Eve a different person from the species' first member?

acceptedAnswers: lineage sorting: most mtDNAs from her contemporaries went extinct; only her lineage survived to leave all modern human mtDNA descendants

hints: Most mt lineages from any era are eventually lost.
steps.reveal: Mt-Eve was simply the woman whose mtDNA lineage happened to survive drift while contemporaries' did not. She lived alongside thousands of other women whose mtDNAs are now extinct. By the coalescent backward, every locus has a different TMRCA + a different 'Eve'/'Adam'. The autosomal coalescent times average ~500 kya; the Y-chromosomal Adam is ~200-300 kya; mt-Eve is ~150-200 kya. They were all real people but ordinary contemporaries of many others — the survival of their lineages was statistical, not selective.

steps.prompt: What was the popular misinterpretation of the 1987 paper?

acceptedAnswers: mt-Eve as a unique progenitor; she was a normal member of a population of thousands

steps.reveal: Cover of *Newsweek* (January 1988) showed an Eve-like figure with a snake — implying mt-Eve was the first woman or a unique progenitor. False: she was an ordinary member of a population of thousands of women, identifiable only retrospectively because her lineage happened to survive while contemporaries' did not. The science is statistical coalescent, not biblical genealogy.

question.finalResult: Mt-Eve TMRCA ≈ 150-200 kya. She was an ordinary member of an African Homo sapiens population whose mtDNA happened to survive drift while contemporaries' did not. Coalescent time = 2N_e (haploid) ≈ 350000 yr matches order of magnitude. The species (Homo sapiens) is older (~300 kya from heidelbergensis); the lineage is older still. Different loci coalesce at different times to different 'Eves'/'Adams' — all statistical, not biblical.

question.question: Why is the Tibetan high-altitude EPAS1 haplotype called one of the most striking examples of adaptive introgression in any species?
options: Tibetans (~6 kya on the plateau) carry a haplotype at the EPAS1 locus (HIF-2α; oxygen sensing) at ~87% frequency. The haplotype confers a blunted polycythemic response to hypoxia (Tibetans have only modestly elevated hemoglobin at 4000 m, avoiding chronic mountain sickness and pregnancy complications associated with high hemoglobin). Huerta-Sánchez et al. (2014 *Nature*) demonstrated the haplotype matches the Denisovan genome (sequenced from Altai) far better than any modern population. So the adaptive Tibetan haplotype was **introgressed from Denisovans** (~40-50 kya) and then driven to high frequency by selection (s ≈ 0.03-0.06) after Tibetan plateau colonization. Modern Han Chinese carry the haplotype at ~9% — consistent with Denisovan introgression into ancestral Asian populations followed by purifying selection or drift in lowland descendants and strong positive selection in Tibetan ancestors. Demonstrates: (1) admixture as source of adaptive variation; (2) standing introgressed variation enabling rapid adaptation; (3) ancient hybridization between hominin species shaped modern adaptive landscapes.
question.explanation: Tibetan EPAS1 high-altitude haplotype (Huerta-Sánchez 2014) was introgressed from Denisovans (~40-50 kya) and then driven to ~87% by recent positive selection in Tibetans (~6 kya plateau colonization). Confers blunted polycythemic response — adaptive at 4000 m. Han Chinese carry it at ~9%; absent elsewhere. Striking adaptive introgression: ancient hybridization with Denisovans provided standing variation that selection later optimized.
hints: Where did the haplotype come from?
question.workedSolution: Tibetan EPAS1 haplotype is Denisovan-introgressed (Huerta-Sánchez 2014) and selected to ~87% over ~6 kya after Tibetan plateau colonization. Blunted polycythemic response is adaptive at altitude. Selection s ≈ 0.03-0.06. Combines ancient hybridization (Denisovan x ancestral Asian ~40-50 kya) + recent local selection. Classic adaptive introgression example.

question.question: Pääbo's Nobel and the technical revolution
question.prompt: Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for sequencing the Neanderthal + Denisovan genomes and establishing ancient DNA as a discipline. Walk through (a) why ancient DNA sequencing was technically nearly impossible before Pääbo's 1980s-2000s methodological work (contamination, fragmentation, deamination, low yield), (b) what changes (silica-extraction, library preparation for degraded DNA, computational removal of cytosine deamination artifacts, single-stranded library construction Meyer 2012) made the Neanderthal genome possible by 2010, and (c) why the discovery that all non-Africans carry 1-4% Neanderthal DNA was unexpected given the prior multiregional-vs-replacement debate.

question.question: Non-African modern humans carry approximately 2% Neanderthal-derived autosomal DNA. If admixture occurred ~50000 years ago (~2000 generations) as one pulse, the initial admixture fraction f satisfies f × (1 - migration loss) ≈ 0.02. Assuming no subsequent gene flow and approximately neutral persistence, what initial admixture fraction f explains current ~2%? (Answer in %.)
question.hint: Under neutral persistence, no decline expected from initial; if no further gene flow + neutrality, f_initial ≈ f_current.

question.prompt: In ≤150 words, explain how the last ~10000 years of human history — agriculture, dairying, urbanization, geographic dispersal, pathogen exposure — have driven some of the strongest selection signals ever measured in our species. Name at least three loci with specific selective contexts.
question.rubric: Should mention: (1) Lactase persistence — regulatory variants upstream of LCT (Bersaglieri 2004 European rs4988235; Tishkoff 2007 East African convergent variants). Drives lactase expression into adulthood; selection coefficient s ≈ 0.05-0.10 (one of strongest in humans); ~10 kya, coincident with cattle domestication; ancient DNA shows rise to dominance in post-Bronze-Age Europe (Mathieson 2015). (2) Skin pigmentation — SLC24A5 (Lamason 2005), SLC45A2, TYR — light skin in high-latitude populations for UVB-driven vitamin D synthesis (Jablonski + Chaplin); convergent at multiple loci in Europeans, South Asians, Middle Easterners. (3) EPAS1 (Yi + Huerta-Sánchez 2014) — Tibetan altitude adaptation; haplotype Denisovan-introgressed, driven to ~87% after plateau colonization. (4) HbS, HbC, Duffy-null, G6PD, thalassemias — malaria-protective; convergent at ≥10 loci in malarial regions; balancing selection (Allison 1954). (5) FOXP2, AMY1, ADH1B, CCR5-Δ32 — various recent sweeps. Sabeti (EHH) + Pritchard (iHS) tools for detection. Recent human evolution has been rapid and ongoing.
